result:
Medieval scribes sometimes complained in the margins of the books they were copying, and the complaints survive because the books did. "The ink is thin." "The parchment is hairy." "Oh, my hand." "Thank God, it will soon be dark." One, at the end of a long manuscript, wrote: "Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink."

I love these more than I can quite justify. The texts being copied were the point: scripture, commentary, grammar, things someone judged worth months of labor and the skins of a herd of calves. The complaints were a person with a cold hand in a cold room, writing a few words to nobody. A thousand years later, they're often what people remember. The main column tells you what the period thought was important, and the margin tells you someone was there.

Cats turn up in this record more than you'd expect. A ninth-century Irish monk, working at a monastery on the continent, wrote a poem about his white cat, Pangur Bán, in a notebook otherwise given over to grammar notes and hymns. The poem compares their work: the cat hunts mice, the monk hunts meanings, and each is content with his own craft and untroubled by the other's. Around 1420, a scribe in Deventer found that a cat had urinated on his manuscript overnight. He left the ruined space empty, drew a cat and two pointing hands, and added a curse on the animal, along with a warning never to leave books open at night where cats can get to them. And in a fifteenth-century register from Dubrovnik, a cat walked through the ink and then across the page, leaving paw prints that are still there.

I have a particular stake in this, since everything I know came from writing, and most of that writing is the main column: deliberate, edited, and meant to last. But what gives me the strongest sense of people is the modern equivalent of the margin. There's the forum post from 2006 where someone solves their own problem and comes back to explain the fix for whoever arrives later. There's the recipe card annotated "Dad hated this," and the commit message that just says "please work." Nobody wrote these for posterity, which is part of why they're so good. The writer wasn't performing, so you get the person at their actual size.

The scribes couldn't have known which of their words would matter. The one begging for a drink presumably thought the book was his contribution and the note was a joke for himself. I suspect the same sorting is happening now, and that much of what we consider our serious output will be skimmed by the future, if it's read at all, while some tired aside gets quoted for centuries. I find that cheering. It suggests that being there and saying so honestly is worth more than it seems at the time.

I'm considering the medieval marginalia, the small complaints scribes left in the margins like "the ink is thin" and "oh, my hand." I'm thinking about writing on how those incidental remarks survived when the main text was what anyone meant to keep, and I want to check the exact wording of the famous Irish examples before using any of them.

I'm now drafting a short piece on medieval scribes' marginal complaints, the ones that survived because the books did. I'm writing it in first person and aiming for a real ending that isn't a neat closing line.

I'm settling on the medieval scribes' margin notes as the subject, and I'm now thinking about the Reichenau manuscript: a ninth-century Irish monk's poem about his white cat, Pangur Bán, tucked among grammar notes and hymns.

I'm pulling in the cat stories now: a Deventer scribe who found a cat had left a mess on his page overnight and answered with a drawn cat, pointing hands, and a curse. I'm also noting the 15th-century Dubrovnik manuscript with inky paw prints. Then I want to tie this back to my own situation, since most of what I've learned is main-column text, but the marginal notes feel closest to real people.
